home.faq_subtitle: Quick answers to common questions about PC bottlenecks and performance issues.

faqs.a: A PC bottleneck happens when one component limits the performance of the whole system. For example, even with a high-end GPU, a weaker CPU may prevent it from reaching full potential.

faqs.q: Is a CPU or GPU bottleneck worse?
faqs.a: Neither is inherently worse. The limiting component changes by game, scene, resolution, and settings. Compare FPS, frame times, per-core CPU load, GPU load, temperatures, and caps before drawing a conclusion.

faqs.q: How accurate is the bottleneck calculator?
faqs.a: Our PC Bottleneck Calculator provides an indicative comparison from normalized component scores. It is not a measured benchmark, and results vary by game, settings, drivers, cooling, and the rest of the system.

faqs.q: Do RAM or storage also cause bottlenecks?
faqs.a: Yes. Insufficient or slow RAM can cause stutters in heavy workloads. Similarly, using an HDD instead of an SSD will lead to slower loading times.

faqs.q: Should CPU and GPU both run at 100%?
faqs.a: There is no universal ideal utilization. High GPU load can be normal in a demanding scene, while overall CPU load can hide one saturated core. Treat utilization as one clue and compare it with frame times, caps, temperatures, and repeated tests.

about.intro_p2: Whether you’re planning a gaming PC, editing workstation, or budget build, use the tools to create a preliminary shortlist, then verify it with manufacturer documentation and workload-specific benchmarks.

about.mission_desc_1: Building or upgrading a PC shouldn’t be a guessing game. PCBuildCheck combines manufacturer-published specifications, internally normalized component scores, and clear explanations to help you compare possible pairings before you buy.
about.mission_desc_2: The goal is to make assumptions and limitations visible so you can compare options more carefully. The tools cannot guarantee compatibility, FPS, value, or a specific upgrade benefit.

faqs.q: How does the FPS calculator work?
faqs.a: The FPS calculator uses a database of component benchmarks and game optimization data to estimate average frames per second you can expect with your selected CPU and GPU combination.

faqs.q: Why is my actual FPS different from the calculator’s estimate?
faqs.a: Real-world FPS can vary due to factors like drivers, cooling, RAM speed, background processes, and specific in-game settings. The calculator provides a baseline estimate for most users.

faqs.q: Can I use the FPS calculator for future games?
faqs.a: While the calculator is based on current benchmark data, it can give a rough idea for upcoming titles. However, new game engines and updates may cause performance to differ.

faqs.q: Does resolution and graphics settings affect FPS results?
faqs.a: Yes. Running games at higher resolutions (1440p, 4K) or ultra settings requires more GPU power, which lowers FPS compared to playing at 1080p or medium settings.

guide.title: Understanding PC Bottlenecks: A Complete Guide to a Balanced System
guide.intro: A bottleneck describes a workload in which one component reaches its limit before another. The limiting component can change with the game, resolution, settings, drivers, and background activity. Our PC Bottleneck Calculator compares internally normalized CPU and GPU scores to help you create a shortlist for further testing.
guide.intro_p2: A score comparison can help you avoid obviously mismatched components, but it cannot predict every workload or guarantee a particular frame rate. Verify important purchase decisions with benchmarks for your games and settings.

cpu_section.title: What is a CPU Bottleneck?
cpu_section.subtitle: (The "Bad" Bottleneck)
cpu_section.description: A CPU bottleneck happens when your processor (CPU) cannot process data and instructions fast enough to keep your graphics card (GPU) fully occupied. This is the most common and problematic type of bottleneck for gamers, as it leads to inconsistent performance that can't be fixed by simply lowering graphics settings.
symptoms_list: Stuttering or choppy gameplay, especially during intense action.
Low FPS in CPU-intensive games (Valorant, Counter-Strike 2, strategy titles).
GPU usage is low (60–70%) while CPU cores are maxed at 100%.

gpu_section.title: What is a GPU Bottleneck?
gpu_section.subtitle: (A workload-specific limit)
gpu_section.description: A GPU-limited test is one where the graphics workload reaches its limit before the CPU. High utilization and FPS changes after lowering graphics settings can support that diagnosis, but no single utilization percentage proves it.
gpu_section.description_p2: Check frame times, clocks, temperatures, power limits, drivers, and an uncapped repeatable scene. A GPU-limited result is not automatically good or bad; it depends on whether the system meets your target.

action_plan.title: How to Fix a Bottleneck: Your Action Plan
action_plan.description: Once our calculator identifies a bottleneck, here are the most effective steps to address it.

cpu_solutions.title: Tackling a CPU Bottleneck
cpu_solutions.intro: If your CPU is the weak link, reduce its workload or boost its performance.
immediate_fixes_list: Close Background Apps: Shut down browsers/streaming apps before gaming.
Lower CPU-Heavy Settings: Reduce physics, crowd density, view distance.
Test Multiple Resolutions: Higher resolution usually increases GPU load and reduces FPS; comparison can help reveal which component reaches its limit first.
long_term_fixes_list: Measure Before Upgrading: Compare frame-time and per-core utilization data in the games you actually use.
Consider Hardware Only After Testing: Compare game-specific benchmarks, platform cost, and measured frame-time issues before choosing a CPU.
cpu_solutions.example_title: Real-World Example: Upgrading Your CPU for a Modern GPU
cpu_solutions.example_desc: A user upgrades to a NVIDIA RTX 4070 but keeps an older Ryzen 5 3600.
cpu_solutions.example_issue: At 1440p/4K it performs decently, but in esports at 1080p, stutters appear regardless of settings.
cpu_solutions.example_solution: The Solution: This is a CPU bottleneck. Upgrading to a Ryzen 5 7600X or Intel Core i5-14600K restores balance, letting the RTX 4070 shine.

gpu_solutions.title: Managing a GPU Bottleneck
gpu_solutions.intro: This is often a good thing. The goal isn’t to remove it, but to tune for your FPS target.
levers_list: Lower GPU settings (textures, shadows, ray tracing).
gpu_solutions.example_title: Real-World Example: Overcoming a Mid-Range GPU Limit
gpu_solutions.example_desc: A Ryzen 5 5600X is paired with an older GTX 1660 Super.
gpu_solutions.example_issue: At 1440p, the CPU can handle the logic, but the GPU maxes out at 100% and struggles to keep smooth FPS.
gpu_solutions.example_solution: The Solution: Upgrade to a RTX 4060 or RX 7700 XT for stable, high-quality 1440p gaming.

final_section.title: How Our Calculator Leads to a Balanced PC
final_section.description: Our tool analyzes component relationships so you don’t have to. By entering your parts, you get instant, data-driven analysis to:
benefits_list: Build Smarter: Avoid pairing a high-end GPU with a weak CPU.
Upgrade with Confidence: Know which part gives biggest gains.
Save Money: Don’t overspend on bottlenecked components.
final_section.cta: Ready to compare your build? Use the calculator for a normalized score comparison, then verify the result with workload-specific benchmarks.

fps_guide.title: Understanding Your Gaming Performance: The FPS Calculator
fps_guide.intro: In the world of PC gaming, Frames Per Second (FPS) is the ultimate measure of performance. It represents how many individual images your computer can display every second, directly translating to the smoothness of your gameplay. A high, stable FPS means a fluid, responsive experience, while a low FPS leads to stuttering and lag.

why_estimate.title: Why Estimate Your FPS?
why_estimate.content: Knowing your potential gaming performance before you buy a new game or upgrade a component is crucial. It empowers you to make informed decisions, manage expectations, and avoid the disappointment of a purchase that your PC can't handle.

how_works.title: How Does the FPS Calculator Work?
how_works.content: Our calculator provides an indicative estimate from normalized CPU and GPU scores. It considers three key factors:
list: Your CPU's Power: The processor handles the game's logic, physics, and AI. In many eSports titles, the CPU is the primary driver of high frame rates.
Your GPU's Power: The graphics card is responsible for rendering the visuals. In graphically intense AAA titles, the GPU does the heaviest lifting.
Your Target Resolution: Playing at 4K requires your GPU to render four times as many pixels as 1080p, which has a massive impact on the final FPS.

low_fps.title: Low FPS? Your Next Steps to a Better Gaming Experience

step1.title: Step 1: Diagnose the Core Issue with Our Bottleneck Calculator
step1.p1: Before you consider an upgrade, you need to know why your FPS is low. Is your powerful GPU being held back by an older CPU? Or is your GPU simply not strong enough for your desired settings?
step1.p2: Our PC Bottleneck Calculator compares internally normalized CPU and GPU scores. Use the relative score gap as a planning clue, not as measured FPS loss or a definitive diagnosis.

step2.title: Step 2: Ensure You Have Enough Power for an Upgrade
step2.p1: If you're planning a GPU upgrade to boost your FPS, there's one critical step you can't ignore: your Power Supply Unit (PSU). Modern graphics cards can be very power-hungry.
step2.p2: Use our PSU Wattage Calculator to ensure your power supply can handle any new hardware you're considering.

readiness.title: Compatibility and power check
readiness.description: Review the platform and power implications of each selected upgrade before making a shortlist.
cpu_checks: Confirm the exact motherboard model, chipset, BIOS version and CPU support list.
Check cooler mounting, thermal capacity and whether the platform requires different RAM.
A matching socket alone does not guarantee motherboard or BIOS compatibility.
gpu_checks: Confirm the PSU maker and GPU board partner's wattage and power-connector guidance.
Check card length, thickness, slot clearance, support bracket and case airflow.
Verify the display outputs, driver support and any required adapter or native cable.
readiness.power_note: Power values use published CPU/GPU figures plus a broad 150 W allowance and 30% planning headroom, rounded up to a common PSU size. They do not model transient spikes, factory limits, PSU age, rail design or connector availability.

upgrade_impact.limitation: Planning estimate only—not a measured benchmark or purchasing recommendation. Verify game-specific tests, motherboard socket and BIOS support, RAM compatibility, case clearance, PSU wattage and connectors before upgrading.

psu_page.faq_subtitle: Quick answers to common questions about choosing the right PSU for your gaming PC.

faqs.q: How does the PSU calculator determine the required wattage?
faqs.a: The calculator combines published CPU and GPU power figures with a broad allowance for other components, then applies 15–50% headroom. It is a planning estimate, not an electrical measurement or certification.

faqs.q: Is it bad to use a PSU with much higher wattage than needed?
faqs.a: A correctly installed, compatible higher-wattage PSU does not force its full rated wattage into the PC. Efficiency varies by model and load, so compare the manufacturer's efficiency curve and connector support rather than relying on a universal utilization target.

faqs.q: Does PSU efficiency (80 Plus rating) affect gaming performance?
faqs.a: PSU efficiency ratings do not directly determine FPS. They describe conversion efficiency under specified test conditions; actual efficiency varies by load, mains voltage, and model.

faqs.q: Can undervaluing PSU wattage cause hardware damage?
faqs.a: An inadequate or poor-quality PSU can contribute to shutdowns or instability. Use this estimate only as a starting point and verify the GPU vendor and board partner's minimum wattage, connector, and power-delivery guidance.

psu_guide.header_title: PSU Wattage Calculator – Find the Right Power Supply for Your Gaming PC
psu_guide.intro: Choosing a suitable Power Supply Unit (PSU) requires more than adding component wattages. An inadequate or poor-quality unit can contribute to shutdowns or instability. Our PSU Calculator provides a planning estimate from published component figures and configurable headroom; it does not replace manufacturer guidance.
psu_guide.why_title: Why Use a PSU Wattage Calculator?
psu_guide.why_desc: Picking a PSU is not just about wattage. Connector support, build quality, form factor, efficiency, transient response, warranty, and the graphics-card maker's guidance also matter. A PSU wattage calculator can narrow the range to research, but it cannot certify compatibility or safety.
psu_guide.how_title: How Does the PSU Calculator Work?
psu_guide.how_desc_1: The tool adds published CPU and GPU power figures to a broad allowance for other selected components. It then displays estimates with 15%, 30%, and 50% headroom. These figures do not fully model transient spikes, factory-overclocked cards, power connectors, PSU age, or model quality.
psu_guide.how_desc_2: Use the result as a shortlist aid, then check the GPU manufacturer and board partner's minimum PSU wattage and connector requirements. The PC Bottleneck Calculator is a separate relative-score comparison and does not determine electrical compatibility.
psu_guide.benefits_title: Benefits of Using Our PSU Calculator
benefits_list: Start with a planning range: Compare several common PSU sizes instead of treating one number as exact.
Compare headroom: See how different allowances change the estimate.
Plan possible upgrades: Consider whether later components may increase the load.
Verify before buying: Confirm wattage, connectors, form factor, and model quality with manufacturer documentation and independent PSU testing.
psu_guide.conclusion_title: Build Smarter with the Right PSU
psu_guide.conclusion_desc: The PSU is an important part of a reliable PC. Use our PSU Wattage Calculator to create a preliminary planning range, then verify the exact graphics card, PSU model, connectors, and manufacturer requirements before purchasing. The FPS Calculator provides separate performance estimates and does not validate power-supply compatibility.
